tips.title: Draw from the shoulder
tips.body: For long lines and big shapes, move your whole arm, not just your wrist. Lines become smoother and more confident.

tips.title: Light first, dark last
tips.body: Start with very light construction lines (HB, light pressure). Darken only the lines you're sure about at the end. Heavy early lines can't be hidden.

tips.title: Horizon before anything
tips.body: In any scene, draw the horizon (eye level) first. Every other decision about perspective depends on it.

tips.title: Heads on the horizon
tips.body: When the viewer stands on flat ground, standing adults' heads sit on the horizon line, near and far. Just draw distant people smaller.

tips.title: Three tones are enough
tips.body: Light, mid and dark. If your drawing has these three clearly separated values, it will look solid, even without detailed shading.

tips.title: Ellipses get rounder away from eye level
tips.body: A cup at eye level is a thin ellipse; the same cup far below your eyes is almost a circle. Check every ellipse against the horizon.

tips.title: Measure with your pencil
tips.body: Hold your pencil at arm's length, elbow locked, and compare one length to another. Proportion errors disappear.

tips.title: Squint to see values
tips.body: Half-close your eyes. Details vanish and the big light and dark shapes appear. Draw those first.

tips.title: Stick → box → body
tips.body: Draw people as a stick figure for the gesture, add boxes for chest and hips, then cylinders for limbs. Faces last, if at all.

tips.title: Overlap creates depth
tips.body: Something drawn in front of something else instantly reads as closer. Use overlap generously in scenes.

tips.title: Vary your line weight
tips.body: Thicker lines for edges in shadow or closer to you; thinner lines for edges in light or far away. One line weight looks flat.

tips.title: Cast shadow anchors objects
tips.body: Without a cast shadow, objects float. A small dark shadow where an object touches the ground plants it firmly.

tips.title: Draw the negative space
tips.body: If a shape is hard (a chair's legs, a hand), draw the empty spaces between parts instead. The object appears by itself.

tips.title: Hands: mitten first
tips.body: Draw the hand as a mitten shape, then split it into fingers. Fingers are three segments that get shorter towards the tip.

tips.title: Texture by mark, not by tone
tips.body: Wood = long wavy lines, stone = dots and cracks, fabric = folds, metal = sharp highlights. Choose the mark for the material.

tips.title: Hatch in one direction
tips.body: Keep hatching strokes in one direction across a shape, or follow its form. Random scribbles look messy.

tips.title: Exaggerate the pose
tips.body: Push a gesture slightly further than it really is. On a small exam sheet, subtle poses don't read.

tips.title: Foreshortened limbs overlap
tips.body: An arm pointing at you is a set of overlapping circles and ellipses, not a long tube. Draw what you see, not what you know.

tips.title: Keep a sketchbook in your bag
tips.body: Ten minutes at a bus stop or in a queue is ten minutes of observation. The habit matters more than the quality.

tips.title: Use reference lines on the sheet
tips.body: Lightly divide your sheet into thirds or frames before drawing. It saves you from cramming the last frame into a corner.

tips.title: Read the whole paper first
tips.body: Spend the first 5 minutes reading every question and writing a finishing time next to each. You'll never get stuck spending 40 minutes on one.

tips.title: Underline the deliverables
tips.body: Count exactly what's asked: 3 frames, 200 words, 4 symbols. Missing a deliverable loses marks you can't recover.

tips.title: Answer the brief, not your favourite idea
tips.body: If the brief says 'for an elderly person', every drawing must show that person's needs. Off-brief beauty scores low.

tips.title: Your second idea is usually better
tips.body: Write down 5 ideas in a minute. The first two are what everyone thinks of. Choose from the rest.

tips.title: Make it readable in 10 seconds
tips.body: Examiners look at hundreds of sheets. A clear focal point, labels and a short caption help your idea land instantly.

tips.title: Finish, then polish
tips.body: Get every question to 'complete and readable' first. Use leftover minutes for shading and details.

tips.title: Labels explain thinking
tips.body: Label what's new or clever ('foldable handle doubles as a stand'), not what's obvious ('chair').

tips.title: Respect word limits
tips.body: Count words when you finish. Going far over a 20-word caption shows you didn't follow the brief.

tips.title: Show the user
tips.body: When designing a product or space, draw a person using it. It proves the solution works for the right user.

tips.title: Indian context wins
tips.body: Steel tumblers, auto-rickshaws, rangoli, local markets: specific Indian details make your work feel observed and real.

tips.title: Don't leave anything blank
tips.body: A 3-minute labelled thumbnail earns marks; a blank space earns nothing. Always attempt everything.

tips.title: Use the whole sheet
tips.body: Plan your layout so drawings use about two-thirds of the area. Tiny drawings look timid; overcrowded ones look rushed.

tips.title: Big idea, simple execution
tips.body: Clever ideas drawn simply beat simple ideas drawn elaborately. Spend thinking time before drawing time.

tips.title: Mistakes are data
tips.body: Write one line in your mistake notebook for every error. Before each mock, read the whole notebook. It takes 5 minutes.

tips.title: Practise in exam conditions
tips.body: At least once a week: phone away, timer on, real A4 sheets, the exact materials you'll carry on exam day.

tips.title: Taper, don't cram
tips.body: In the last days before the exam, do lighter practice and sleep well. A rested mind draws faster and thinks clearer.

tips.title: Pack your kit the night before
tips.body: Admit card, ID, pencils, eraser, sharpener, scale, colours (if allowed), water. Check the list twice, then sleep.

tips.title: Objective questions: one pass
tips.body: If an objective section appears, move fast and mark doubtful ones. Never let one puzzle eat 3 minutes.

tips.title: Guess smart
tips.body: When unsure in an objective question, eliminate options you know are wrong first. Your odds improve dramatically.

tips.title: Mains is about thinking aloud
tips.body: In the studio test and interview, examiners want to see how you think. Explain your choices calmly and simply.

tips.title: 1.8 minutes per mark
tips.body: 180 minutes ÷ 100 marks ≈ 1.8 minutes per mark, minus reading and checking time. A 20-mark question is worth about 32 minutes.

tips.title: Watch the clock at every finish line
tips.body: Look at the clock each time you finish a question. If you're behind, simplify the next answer instead of rushing the last one.

tips.title: The 20% rule
tips.body: If a question runs 20% over its planned time, stop, label it, and move on. Come back only if time remains.

tips.title: Thumbnails save time
tips.body: A 1-minute thumbnail of your layout prevents 10 minutes of redrawing later.

tips.title: Short daily practice beats long weekly practice
tips.body: Forty-five minutes every day builds more skill than five hours on Sunday. Consistency compounds.

tips.title: Board-exam balance
tips.body: During board-exam weeks, protect 20 minutes a day for sketching and observation. Your design skill stays warm without hurting your boards.

tips.title: Last 10 minutes are for checking
tips.body: Use the last 10 minutes to add missing labels, captions and question numbers on every sheet.

tips.title: Batch your materials
tips.body: Keep sharpened pencils, eraser and scale in one pouch. Searching for things wastes minutes and focus.

tips.title: Notice one bad design a day
tips.body: On your way to school, find one thing that's annoying to use. Ask: who suffers, why, and what would fix it?

tips.title: Watch hands
tips.body: Watch how people hold things: tools, phones, cups, bags. Hands show you exactly where a design works or fails.

tips.title: Collect details
tips.body: Fill a sketchbook page with small details: door handles, signboards, vegetable stalls, footwear. They make memory drawings convincing.

tips.title: Look at light at different hours
tips.body: The same street looks different at 8 am, 1 pm and 5 pm. Notice shadow length and direction.

tips.title: Observe queues and crowds
tips.body: Where do people bunch up? Where do they wait awkwardly? Crowds reveal bad planning instantly.

tips.title: Watch the elderly and children
tips.body: Designs that work for grandparents and small children usually work for everyone. Observe what they struggle with.

tips.title: Read signs critically
tips.body: For every sign you see today, ask: could I understand it in 2 seconds without reading? Why or why not?

tips.title: Study packaging
tips.body: Before throwing away a packet, look at how it opens, what it protects and how much waste it creates.

tips.title: Notice colour in markets
tips.body: Vendors arrange fruit and flowers in colour groups. Look at which colours they put side by side and why it attracts you.

tips.title: Listen to a place
tips.body: Close your eyes for one minute at a busy spot. Sounds tell you about activity, time and mood, useful for audio-visual tasks.

tips.title: Look up
tips.body: Most people never look above eye level. Balconies, wires, signboards and trees above you are rich drawing material.

tips.title: Touch materials
tips.body: Feel cane, clay, cloth, metal and wood. Knowing how materials behave helps in the studio sensitivity test.

tips.title: Watch how things are repaired
tips.body: Cobblers, cycle mechanics and tailors are brilliant problem-solvers. Their tools and tricks are design lessons.

tips.title: SCAMPER any object
tips.body: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse. Seven questions, seven new ideas.

tips.title: Ask '5 whys'
tips.body: Keep asking why a problem happens until you reach a cause you can design for. Solve the root, not the symptom.

tips.title: Give your user a name
tips.body: Instead of 'an elderly person', imagine 'Lakshmi, 72, uses a stick, lives on the 2nd floor'. Specific users give specific ideas.

tips.title: List properties before uses
tips.body: For 'uses of a bottle', first list: hollow, transparent, light, has a cap, rolls, holds water. Each property unlocks new uses.

tips.title: Combine two unrelated things
tips.body: Many good ideas are two things put together: a bench + a planter, an umbrella + a light. Try forced combinations.

tips.title: Think of extremes
tips.body: What would this look like for a child? For a giant? In zero gravity? Extremes shake you out of the obvious.

tips.title: Steal from nature
tips.body: Bamboo's nodes, a leaf's veins, a shell's spiral: nature has solved many design problems. Ask how nature would do it.

tips.title: Mind-map for 2 minutes
tips.body: Write the topic in the centre and branch out quickly. The connection between two distant branches is often the idea.

tips.title: Reverse the problem
tips.body: Instead of 'how to keep a classroom quiet', ask 'how to make it as noisy as possible', then flip each answer.

tips.title: Visual metaphors
tips.body: Show an abstract idea with an object: time as a melting ice cube, unity as tied ropes. Metaphors make posters memorable.

tips.title: Quantity first
tips.body: Aim for 10 rough ideas before judging any. Judging early kills good ideas before they grow.

tips.title: Design for the context
tips.body: The same product changes in a hospital, a farm and a festival. Always ask: where exactly will this be used?

tips.title: Number every sheet
tips.body: Write the question number clearly on every sheet. Examiners shouldn't have to guess.

tips.title: Neat block capitals
tips.body: Small, even block capitals with a light guideline look professional and are easy to read.

tips.title: Leader lines that don't cross
tips.body: Draw label lines with a scale if possible, and never let them cross each other.

tips.title: One focal point per frame
tips.body: In each storyboard frame or poster, decide the ONE thing the eye should see first and make it the biggest or darkest.

tips.title: Frames with borders
tips.body: Draw clean frame borders for storyboards. Consistent frame sizes make a sequence feel organised.

tips.title: Colour with restraint
tips.body: Two or three colours used deliberately look stronger than ten colours used everywhere.

tips.title: Photograph your models well
tips.body: Plain background, side light from a window, three angles plus one close-up of the cleverest joint.

tips.title: One sheet, one story
tips.body: When presenting work, use one sheet with big visuals and few words. You are the explanation.

tips.title: Sleep is practice
tips.body: Your brain consolidates drawing skill and memory while you sleep. Seven to eight hours is part of the training.

tips.title: 20-20-20 for your eyes
tips.body: Every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

tips.title: Stretch your drawing hand
tips.body: Open and close your fist ten times and rotate your wrists between long drawing sessions.

tips.title: Tough day? Do the minimum
tips.body: On a hard day, switch on tough-day mode and do half. Showing up keeps the habit alive; guilt doesn't help.

tips.title: Drink water, eat on time
tips.body: Long drawing sessions drain energy. Keep water nearby and don't skip meals before practice or mocks.

tips.title: Compare with yesterday, not with others
tips.body: Look at your Day 1 sheet next to today's. That's the only comparison that matters.

tips.title: Move every hour
tips.body: A five-minute walk resets focus. Many designers get ideas while walking.

tips.title: Calm before the exam
tips.body: The night before the exam, stop practising by evening. Pack your bag, eat a normal dinner and sleep early.

tips.title: Boards and NID can co-exist
tips.body: Short daily design practice is a break from board revision, not a burden. Keep it light and fun this month.

tips.title: Talk to someone
tips.body: If you feel stressed for several days, tell GB or a friend. Talking about it shrinks the worry.

tips.title: Point, example, close
tips.body: Answer interview questions in three parts: your main point, one example from your life, and a one-line conclusion.

tips.title: Know your own work
tips.body: Be ready to explain why you made every choice in your portfolio and models. 'It looked nice' isn't enough.

tips.title: It's okay to pause
tips.body: A two-second pause to think sounds more confident than filling silence with 'umm'.

tips.title: Talk about what you noticed
tips.body: Interviewers love genuine observations about everyday life. Bring stories from your town, family and travels.

tips.title: Know NID
tips.body: Founded in 1961 in Ahmedabad, inspired by the India Report (1958) by Charles and Ray Eames. Know why that history matters to you.

tips.title: Be honest about weaknesses
tips.body: Saying 'my perspective drawing was weak, so I practised a page of boxes every day' shows maturity.

tips.title: Explain your model in 60 seconds
tips.body: Practise: what the brief asked → what you understood → your idea → why these materials → what you'd improve.

tips.title: Studio test: play with materials first
tips.body: Before building, spend a few minutes testing how the material bends, folds and joins. The best ideas come from the material.

tips.title: Make it stand
tips.body: In model-making, stability matters. Triangles, folds and wide bases keep structures upright.

tips.title: Craftsmanship shows care
tips.body: Clean cuts, hidden glue and straight edges tell examiners you respect your work.

tips.title: Draw boxes daily
tips.body: Fill half a page with boxes in two-point perspective every day for a week. Everything else in perspective gets easier.

tips.title: Cylinders and cones everywhere
tips.body: Bottles, cups, lamp posts, pots, people's arms: most objects are cylinders and cones. Master these two forms.

tips.title: Draw what you see, not what you know
tips.body: You know a plate is round, but from a seat it's an ellipse. Trust your eyes over your knowledge.

tips.title: Crowds in layers
tips.body: Draw crowds as three layers: detailed people in front, simpler shapes in the middle, just heads at the back.

tips.title: Use a pencil grid for symbols
tips.body: For symbol and logo questions, sketch on a light grid so shapes stay balanced and crisp.

tips.title: Posters: headline, image, details
tips.body: Give every poster a clear order: headline first, image second, small details last.

tips.title: Social media series = one system
tips.body: In a 3-post series keep layout, colours and fonts the same, and change only the content. That's what makes it a series.

tips.title: Signage needs placement
tips.body: Every signage answer should show where the sign goes and at what height. Most students forget this.

tips.title: Storyboards need camera changes
tips.body: Mix wide, medium and close-up shots in a storyboard. It feels like a film and holds attention.

tips.title: Write like a designer
tips.body: In 200-word write-ups, talk about form, material, use, user and feeling, plus one improvement.

tips.title: 3 uses: one property each
tips.body: In '3 uses in 3 contexts' questions, give each use a different property of the object so the ideas don't repeat.

tips.title: Symbols: verbs, not nouns
tips.body: For symbol creation, think about what an object does (binds, grows, cuts, lifts). Verbs lead to meanings.

tips.title: Prepare a mental library
tips.body: Keep a list of 20 Indian scenes you can draw from memory: bus stand, market, temple, classroom, kitchen. Practise each once.

tips.title: Weekly mock review
tips.body: After every mock, write three lines: what took too long, what you'd skip, what you'd do first next time.

tips.title: Celebrate small wins
tips.body: Finished a hard mock? Logged a 7-day streak? Take a moment to enjoy it before moving on.

tips.title: Captions add what drawings can't
tips.body: Use captions for time, sound, feelings or reasons, the things a still image can't show.

tips.title: Light source arrow
tips.body: Before shading, draw a tiny arrow in the corner showing where the light comes from. Then stay consistent.

tips.title: Ask 'who else?'
tips.body: Every design affects more than one person: the user, the maker, the cleaner, the neighbour. List them all.

tips.title: Photograph less, sketch more
tips.body: A photo records; a sketch makes you understand. When something interests you, draw it for 2 minutes.
